The VNAV DESCENT page assists in achieving descent by supplying the target velocity and altitude according to descent and velocity limitations. It provides VPATH, VFLC, and other normal descent modes. VPATH mode specifically controls the descent by managing the Vertical Path Angle (VPA).

If the altitude constraint requires the aircraft to cross the waypoint AT the specified altitude, or AT OR ABOVE the specified altitude, the aircraft holds the specified altitude until arrival at the waypoint. If the altitude constraint requires the aircraft to cross the waypoint BETWEEN two altitudes, the lower altitude is held. If the altitude constraint requires the aircraft to cross the waypoint AT OR BELOW the specified altitude, no altitude will be held. When the aircraft is within the capture distance of a constraint altitude, the VNAV mode automatically switches to altitude hold, and remains in altitude hold until the descent is resumed.

The Stall Protection System provides a stick pushing function which can be overridden by pressing the A/P-A/T-S/P DISC Switch on the Flight Control Panel. Pitch (PTCH) Mode will be activated automatically when the Autoflight System is energized and the FD is engaged for the first time. It is the default vertical mode if no other vertical modes are selected. It is also the default vertical mode if a lateral mode is activated before a vertical mode is selected. Engaging the AP when both FDs are disengaged will activate the PTCH Mode.

The Altitude Select (ALTS) Mode is always armed except when ALT, GS, or GA Mode is active, and it is armed when GA Mode is active if the preselected altitude is greater than the current altitude by 75 ft. When VNAV CLIMB encounters an altitude constraint, it holds that altitude until the constraint is cleared. If the constraint requires crossing a waypoint at a specific altitude, or at or below it, that altitude is held. If the constraint is between two altitudes, the higher altitude is held. If the constraint is at or above a specific altitude, no altitude is held. VNAV honors only climb constraints during the climb phase. When approaching a constraint, VNAV sequences to VALTS, VALTV, or VALT until climb resumes. If the preselect altitude is not raised to the flight plan target altitude or above, the preselected altitude will be captured, sequencing the mode to VALTS. VNAV will not sequence to climb VFLC until a climb mode selection is made after the preselect altitude is raised.

Stall alert, stall protection and auto-ignition functions.

The Stall Protection System (SPS) includes two Angle of Attack (AOA) Sensors integrated with Stall Protection Computers (SPC), two stick shakers, and one stick pusher integrated in the AP pitch servo. Each SPC can independently initiate stall alert, stall protection, and auto-ignition. The SPC commands the AP pitch servo motor to activate the stick pusher. The stick pusher function can be inhibited by the A/P-A/T-S/P DISC Switch on the Flight Control Panel (FCP) or the AP/SP DISC Pushbutton on the control wheel. The A/P-A/T-S/P DISC Switch in the down position inhibits the stick pusher function and displays STICK PUSHER NOT AVAIL on EICAS. When the AP/SP DISC Pushbutton is pressed during stick pusher activation, it stops the pushing action on the control column. If both stall protection computers fail, stall alert, stick pushing, and auto-ignition are lost.

When the STALL ADVANCE Switch on the overhead panel of the cockpit is pushed, the Stall Protection System (SPS) enters the Advance Protection Mode, enhancing the stall alert, stall protection, and auto-ignition AOA threshold.

The Stall Protection System (SPS) calculates AOA thresholds for stall alert, stall protection, and automatic ignition based on inputs such as Angle of Attack (AOA), FLAP angle, Airspeed/Mach number, normal and side overload, ice signal, WING A/I Switch signal, STALL ADVANCE Switch, and WOW Signal. When the current AOA reaches a stall alert threshold, the SPS generates stall alert, stall shaker, and pusher commands. The stick pusher activates when both SPCs generate stall pusher commands simultaneously. If AOA continues to increase after stick shakers activate, the Stall Protection Computer (SPC) sends a push command to the pitch servo, moving the control column forward to prevent a stall. The stick pusher deactivates when the airframe AOA is less than the pusher threshold decreased by 0.8°, or normal overload is less than 0.5g, whichever occurs first.

The Autoflight System automatically manages and controls the lateral and vertical flight path of the aircraft using information from the flight plan, FMS, radio navigation aids, or pilot input. It achieves this control through pitch and roll servo mechanisms commanded by the Flight Guidance (FG) system, and automatic thrust control commands from the Autothrottle (AT). The Flight Director (FD) displays these commands on the PFD, and the Flight Control Panel (FCP), control wheel, and thrust levers house most of the associated controllers.

The Autoflight System controls the aircraft's pitch through the pitch servo, generating commands to hold the actual aircraft pitch angle at the selected mode's reference. The pitch angle reference can be adjusted using the PITCH/VS Wheel within a range of -15° to 20°. The AP pitch control is limited between 20° nose up and -15° nose down. In PTCH Mode, the Autothrust (AT) controls airspeed.

The Altitude Select (ALTS) Mode is armed except when ALT, GS, or GA Mode is active. If the vertical mode is GA, ALTS is armed if the preselected altitude is greater than the current altitude by 75 ft. Rotating the ALT knob on the FCP inhibits ALTS Mode to prevent altitude capture during preselected altitude changes. ALTS Mode deselects if ALT, GS, or GA Mode is activated.

In VS Mode, the Autoflight System commands to maintain a preselected vertical speed. The PITCH/VS Wheel on the Flight Control Panel is used to adjust this vertical speed reference, with slow rotation changing it by 100 ft/min per click and quick rotation by more than 100 ft/min per click. The vertical speed reference is capped at ±8000 ft/min. When VS Mode is active, the Autothrottle (AT) controls airspeed.

- Overspeed (OSPD) Mode: Hold fixed indicated airspeed or Mach number.
- Underspeed (USPD) Mode: Hold fixed indicated airspeed or Mach number.

The creation and deletion of waypoints, the change of flight plan, parallel offset, holding pattern, operation in high latitudes, and alternate airports.

The chapter covers the creation and deletion of waypoints, flight plan changes, parallel offsets, holding patterns, operations in high latitudes, and alternate airport procedures. Specific methods for adding waypoints include inserting a waypoint directly, creating flyover waypoints, inserting/adding direct waypoints, creating pilot-defined waypoints (including Along-Track Offset (ATO) and Place Bearing/Distance (PBD) waypoints), and editing FROM waypoints. Deleting discontinuities is also addressed.

Discontinuities represent a break in a flight plan sequence and are used to isolate changed portions of a flight plan during edits. They can be deleted using a DELETE command from the scratchpad or by inserting the next applicable waypoint. Deleting a discontinuity creates a Direct-To course to the next waypoint. However, some discontinuities, such as those before a radar-vectored approach initial leg, at the end of an airway where the next waypoint is not on that airway, or before a leg without a defined starting point, cannot be deleted with the DEL key. Deletion can be performed on the ACT LEGS or ACT FPLN pages by entering "DELETE" or the next waypoint in the scratchpad and then pressing the LSK adjacent to the discontinuity.

Discontinuities can be deleted from a flight plan using a DELETE command from the scratchpad, or by inserting the next applicable waypoint at the discontinuity prompts. Some discontinuities, such as those before an approach with initial radar vectors, at the end of an airway where the next waypoint isn't on that airway, or before a leg without a defined start point (e.g., DME-arc), cannot be deleted with the DEL key.

To delete a discontinuity on the LEGS page:
1. Enter the ACT/MOD LEGS page.
2. Press the DEL key, showing "DELETE" in the scratchpad, or press the LSK for the next applicable waypoint, showing the waypoint in the scratchpad.
3. Press the LSK adjacent to the prompt boxes above the DISCONTINUITY.
4. Press EXEC to make the change effective.

To delete a discontinuity on the FPLN page:
1. Enter the ACT/MOD FPLN page.
2. Press the DEL key, showing "DELETE" in the scratchpad, or press the LSK for the next applicable waypoint, showing the waypoint in the scratchpad.
3. Press the LSK adjacent to the prompt boxes above the DISCONTINUITY.
4. Press EXEC to make the change effective.

If deleting a discontinuity causes an unwanted effect, further flight plan changes may be necessary. To remove legs following a discontinuity, select the downtrack waypoint and enter it into the THEN prompt of the discontinuity; this will replace the discontinuity and delete intermediate waypoints.
When a discontinuity is deleted, a Direct-To course is created to the next waypoint in the flight plan.

Pitch (PTCH) Mode is the basic vertical mode of the Autoflight System where the Flight Guidance (FG) generates commands to maintain the selected aircraft pitch angle. The pitch angle reference can be adjusted between -15° and 20° using the PITCH/VS Wheel.

Engagement Methods:
*   When the Autoflight System is energized and the Flight Director (FD) is engaged for the first time, PTCH Mode will activate automatically.
*   If no other vertical modes are selected, PTCH Mode is the default vertical mode.
*   If a lateral mode is activated before a vertical mode is selected, PTCH Mode is the default.
*   Engaging the Autopilot (AP) when both FDs are disengaged activates PTCH Mode.
*   Turning the PITCH/VS Wheel will activate PTCH Mode in Altitude Select (ALTS), Altitude Hold (ALT), Flight Level Change (FLC), Go-around (GA), PATH Angle, Glidepath (GP), or Overspeed (OSPD) Modes (when not in overspeed).

Deselection Methods:
*   Selecting other vertical modes will deselect PTCH Mode.

The Altitude Select (ALTS) Mode captures the preselected barometric altitude. It is always armed except when the Altitude Hold (ALT) Mode, Glide Slope (GS) Mode, or Go-around (GA) Mode is active. The ALTS Mode is deselected if the ALT Mode, GS Mode, or GA Mode is activated.

Flight Level Change (FLC) Mode is used to hold airspeed or Mach number during climb or descent. Vertical Navigation (VNAV) Mode allows the Autoflight System to follow FMS vertical profile constraints and provides references for these modes, automatically selecting ALTS, ALT, VS, or FLC based on flight plan vertical constraints.

The Glidepath (GP) mode is a vertical mode that is armed white on the FMA and is used to track the glideslope during an approach. It can be disengaged by disengaging AP and FDs, pressing the APPR button, selecting other lateral modes, changing the navigation source, readjusting the frequency of the navigation source, or changing the FG coupled side.

Overspeed Protection Mode is active when the aircraft indicated airspeed is above Vmo + 5 kt or Mach number is above Mmo + 0.01, and it prevents the speed from exceeding Vmo/Mmo. Underspeed Protection Mode is active when the aircraft indicated airspeed is below Vman - 5 kt or Mach number is below Mman - 0.01, and it prevents stall by increasing airspeed.

When the airspeed is below Vmo + 5 kt or Mmo + 0.01, OSPD Mode can be canceled by selecting another vertical mode manually. Or, the OSPD Mode will cancel automatically if the airspeed decreases to Vmo/Mmo.

The primary flight control system is a fly-by-wire system. The pilot sends control signals to the Actuator Control Electronics (including Primary Actuator Control Electronics (P-ACE), Spoiler Actuator Control Electronics (S-ACE) and Horizontal Stabilizer Actuator Control Electronics (HS-ACE)) through the cockpit control inputs. The Actuator Control Electronics combine the control input signals with the sensitivity signals from the Flight Control Cabinet (FCC), and then send a command signals to the actuator servos to move the related control surface. The sensitivity signals and augmentation commands from the Flight Control Cabinet (FCC) are calculated based on the data from the aircraft sensors and adjust the pilot control commands.

The Overspeed (OSPD) Mode automatically activates when the aircraft Mach number exceeds Mmo + 0.01 or airspeed exceeds Vmo + 5 kt. The FMS continually updates the predicted Top of Climb (TOC) location and predicted altitude intercept at the constraint waypoint. If the predicted altitude intercept at the constraint waypoint violates the altitude constraint, amber UNABLE NEXT ALT message is displayed on the CDU, the flight mode annunciator ALT is crossed out on the PDF, and an amber MSG flashes on the PFD. If the aircraft is at a constraint altitude and the preselected altitude is raised, the flight plan target altitude is above the current flight altitude, and an altitude change mode (FLC, VS, or PTCH) is selected, VNAV allows the aircraft to leave the constraint altitude. But if the constraint is an AT, AT OR BELOW, or BETWEEN altitude, the message CHECK FPLN ALT is displayed on the CDU. This message also annunciates when the VNAV selection is made while the aircraft is above the next climb constraint altitude.

The EICAS displays aileron trim, rudder trim, and horizontal stabilizer trim information. For aileron and rudder trim, the display includes trim direction (white LWD/RWD or NL/NR) and trim value. For horizontal stabilizer trim, it shows trim direction (white NU/ND) and trim value. The color of the trim value indicates different conditions: Green signifies normal trim on the ground (within 1.0 for aileron/rudder, within the takeoff green band for horizontal stabilizer) or normal trim in flight. White indicates trim greater than 1.0 on the ground (not in takeoff configuration) or normal trim in flight. Red indicates trim greater than 1.0 on the ground during takeoff configuration. Magenta or dashes signify invalid data.

White LWD (Left Wing Down) or RWD (Right Wing Down) for aileron trim indicates that the aircraft is on the ground and is not in takeoff configuration with the trim value greater than 1.0, or the aircraft is in flight. White NL (Nose Left) or NR (Nose Right) for rudder trim indicates the same conditions.

V1: Takeoff Decision Speed. The speed from which a decision to continue the takeoff, following a failure of the critical engine at VEF, results in a takeoff distance to a height of 35 ft at V2 speed not exceeding the takeoff distance available (TODA), or, in case of rejected takeoff, the distance to bring the aircraft to a full stop not exceed the accelerate-stop distance available (ASDA).
VR: Rotation Speed. The speed from which a decision to continue the takeoff, following a failure of the critical engine at VEF, results in a takeoff distance to a height of 35 ft at V2 speed.
V2: Takeoff Safety Speed. The target speed to be attained at the 35 ft height, assuming recognition of one engine failure at V1 and the decision to continue is taken.
VFTO: Last Takeoff Speed. The last takeoff safety speed reached at the end of the takeoff flight path.

In Automatic Refueling Mode, set the REFUEL SELECTION Switch to AUTO. Use the INCR/DECRT Switch to set the required refuel quantity. Manually open the Refuel Shutoff Valve to start refueling. The Fuel Quantity Computer (FQC) monitors the process and automatically closes the Refuel Shutoff Valve when the preselected quantity is reached. The FQC automatically records and displays the last preselected refuel quantity. Even if the quantity is the same as displayed, operating the INCR/DECRT Switch is necessary to activate the FQC for automatic refueling. Automatic refueling ensures fuel quantities between left and right fuel tanks are balanced. If an imbalance of more than 400 kg (882 lb) occurs, the tank with the higher quantity will be shut off, and when balanced, both tanks will be refueled. Refueling is completed when the combined total equals the preselected value. The High Level Float Pilot Valve will also close the Refuel Shutoff Valve when the aircraft reaches its maximum refueling quantity.

The refueling personnel can open and close the Refuel Shutoff Valve via the TANK REFUELING Switch on the Refuel/defuel Control Panel. This differs from automatic refueling where the Fuel Quantity Computer (FQC) automatically controls the Refuel Shutoff Valve to close when the preselected quantity is reached, and the REFUEL SELECTION Switch is set to AUTO. The manual shutoff function overrides the automatic shutoff function, allowing refueling to be stopped manually even in automatic mode.

TCAS-equipped aircraft can interact with ground-based ATC by the ATC transponder replying to interrogations from ATC. The transponder automatically responds to interrogations of modes A, C, and S, providing the aircraft's ATC 4-digit code, barometric altitude, and Mode S capabilities like the 24-bit access code. Mode S specifically allows for one-to-one interrogation and reply communications with ground stations.

TCAS detects potential collision targets by interrogating other aircraft transponders, determining their relative bearing, range, closure rate, and relative altitude. It then computes their trajectory, Closest Point of Approach (CPA), and estimated time to reach the CPA. When a collision threat is presented, TCAS displays these potential and predicted collision targets.
Its relative bearing, its range and closure rate, and its relative altitude.
TCAS computes the range, range rate, relative bearing, and relative altitude of intruder aircraft.

When the relative position of the intruder presents a collision threat, aural and visual alerts are triggered. TCAS optimizes vertical orders to ensure sufficient trajectory separation and a variable minimal vertical speed considering all intruders.
The classifications of potential collision targets detected by TCAS are Traffic Advisory (TA), Preventive Resolution Advisory (PRA), and Corrective Resolution Advisory (CRA).
TCAS detects proximate aircraft within 6 NM laterally and ± 1200 ft vertically. It displays this proximate traffic as a filled cyan diamond on the PFD/MFD.

Traffic Advisory (TA) informs the pilot of proximate traffic that does not currently constitute a threat but may become one if conditions change. TAU signifies the Time to Until Alert, which is about 40 seconds for a Traffic Advisory (TA).

The LEGS page displays waypoints and segments in the flight plan, including SIDS, STARS, and approach conditional waypoints. Data rows show waypoints, with FROM waypoints in cyan, TO waypoints in magenta, and other waypoints in white. Above each waypoint row, signage shows the azimuth and distance between waypoints, along with information specific to different leg types. The page also displays the distance from the aircraft's current position to the waypoint and vertical navigation information, such as descent angle, reference airspeed, and constraint altitudes or flight levels.

The LEGS page displays the LAST waypoint passed, including the distance from the last waypoint and the time of passage; the TO waypoint, including the distance and time-to-go to the waypoint, and the ETA at the waypoint; the NEXT waypoint after the TO waypoint, including the distance and time-to-go to the waypoint, and the ETA at the waypoint; the DEST (Destination) airport, including the distance and time-to-go to the destination, and the ETA at the destination; FUEL available at the destination airport; and GW of the aircraft at the destination airport.

**Mode 6: Altitude Callouts and Excessive Bank Angle**
*   **Altitude Callouts:** Below 1000 ft AGL, TAWS provides altitude callouts through loudspeakers. The "MINIMUMS" aural alert is provided when descending at the Minimum Descent Altitude (MDA).
*   **Excessive Bank Angle:** If the bank angle is excessive, the aural alert "BANK ANGLE, BANK ANGLE" sounds.

**Mode 3: Altitude Loss After Takeoff**
*   **Condition:** Altitude loss occurs after takeoff or during go-around.
*   **Aural Alert:** "DON'T SINK" sounds.
*   **Inhibition:** The alert stops when the vertical speed returns to a positive value for more than 1 second.

**Mode 7: Reactive Windshear Detection**
*   **Condition:** Aircraft performance degrades to a predetermined threshold due to hazardous microbursts or similar windshear events at low altitude, or when TAWS detects windshear that improves aircraft performance.
*   **Aural Alert:** TAWS triggers an aural alert to notify the flight crew of degraded aircraft performance or potential encountered windshear.
*   **Availability:** The alerting algorithm is active during takeoff and approach.

**General Inhibition:**
*   The TAWS TERR Switch being set to OFF inhibits all Collision Prediction Alerting (CPA) functions and terrain display.
*   The TAWS FLAP Switch being set to OFF inhibits the flap configuration alerting function during landing (Mode 4).
*   The TAWS G/S Switch, when pushed between 30 ft and 1000 ft AGL with G/S and LOC signals received, inhibits the TAWS G/S alert function, indicated by the "OFF" light illuminating. This inhibition automatically cancels when the aircraft flies beyond the 30 ft to 1000 ft altitude range.

The FMS will automatically exit the holding pattern at the hold fix waypoint and continue on the flight plan path when exit conditions are met. The aircraft will exit the hold in one of three ways:
* If the aircraft is already on the inbound turn or inbound leg of the hold, the aircraft exits the hold along the existing holding track at the hold FIX waypoint.
* If the aircraft is on the outbound turn, the FMS continues the turn through the outbound leg heading and back to the holding FIX.
* If the aircraft is on the outbound leg of the hold before the inbound turn, the FMS starts an immediate turn to the inbound leg to exit the hold at the hold FIX.
If the aircraft is on the outbound turn, the FMS continues the turn through the outbound leg heading and back to the holding FIX.

The ARJ21 aircraft's engines include a low-pressure compressor/turbine and a high-pressure compressor/turbine. They also feature a single annular combustor with fuel injector nozzles and ignitors. The accessory gearbox, driven by the high-pressure rotor, powers components like the starter, integrated drive generator, engine-driven pump, permanent magnet alternator, fuel pump, and oil pump. The engine oil system lubricates and cools engine bearings and the accessory gearbox, and also heats fuel to prevent ice formation.

TCAS detects aircraft equipped with transponders within a 30-40 NM lateral range and 9900 ft altitude range. It displays potential and predicted collision targets, issues vertical maneuvering indications, and can show up to 30 aircraft simultaneously. TCAS is independent of ground-based ATC. The system includes a receiver/transmitter and two directional antennas. Controls are located on the RTU, allowing selection of modes like TA/RA, STBY, and TA ONLY, as well as altitude display (REL/ABS) and monitoring of non-threat traffic (ON/OFF). The MFD and PFD display TCAS information, including traffic symbols, altitudes, and advisory messages (TA/RA). TCAS self-test can be performed on the ground. When ATC is de-energized or altitude reporting is OFF, a TCAS FAIL or TCAS OFF message is displayed respectively. TCAS interrogates transponders to determine an intruder's relative bearing, range, closure rate, and relative altitude, then computes trajectory and Closest Point of Approach (CPA) to trigger alerts if a collision threat exists.
